title: Split Array With Same Average
statement:
You are given an array `a` of `n` non-negative integers. Decide whether the elements can be divided into two **non-empty** groups `A` and `B` (every element goes to exactly one group) such that the average of the values in `A` equals the average of the values in `B`.

Print `true` if such a split exists and `false` otherwise.

Elements are distinguished by position, so equal values at different positions can be placed in different groups. If the array has a single element, no split into two non-empty groups exists.

For example, `[1, 2, 3, 4]` can be split into `{1, 4}` and `{2, 3}`, both with average 2.5, but `[1, 4, 2]` cannot: the three possible single-element groups have averages 1, 2 and 4, while the remaining two elements average 3, 2.5 and 1.5.

An important observation: if both groups have the same average, then each also has the same average as the whole array.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` space-separated integers `a[0], ..., a[n-1]`.

examples.explanation: The groups {1, 4} and {2, 3} both have average 2.5.
The groups {2, 4} and {3} both have average 3.
Putting a single element alone gives averages 1, 4 or 2, against 3, 1.5 or 2.5 for the other group. None match.

complexity.time: O(n^2 * S) with bitsets, or O(2^(n/2) * n) meet in the middle

hints: If a group of size `k` has the same average as the whole array, then its sum must be `total * k / n`. This must be an integer, which rules out most values of `k` immediately.
It is enough to look at groups of size `k` with `1 <= k <= n / 2`: the complement of a valid group is valid too, and one of the two has size at most `n / 2`.

Compute, for every size `k`, the set of sums reachable by choosing exactly `k` elements (a subset-sum DP over counts). A Python integer used as a bitset, shifted left by each element, makes this fast. Then check the needed sum for each valid `k`.
